pr_title: planner: generate physical plan for IndexMergePath
pr_body:
<!--
Thank you for contributing to TiDB! Please read TiDB's [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/pingcap/tidb/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md) document **BEFORE** filing this PR.
-->

### What problem does this PR solve? <!--add issue link with summary if exists-->
Fix #11113. 
### What is changed and how it works?
When meeting the `IndexMergePath` in `(ds *DataSource) findBestTask` , it will call function `convertToIndexMergeScan()`  to generate the physical plan for the path.
### Check List <!--REMOVE the items that are not applicable-->

Tests <!-- At least one of them must be included. -->
 - No code

Code changes
 - Has exported function/method change
Add `convertToIndexMergeScan()` and `getIndexMergeCandidate()` in `planner/core/find_best_task.go`. 
Modify some codes in `(ds *DataSource) findBestTask` and `skylinePruning()`, and some related functions for `copTask`.
 - Has exported variable/fields change
 Add `PhysicalIndexMergeReader` to present the physical plan for` IndexMergePath`.

Side effects

 - Possible performance regression

Related changes

review_comments: We need to combine this table scan into the above one.
Of course, we need a `PhysicalTableScan` because `IndexMergePath` must be double read. `partPath`, there, is used to get `rowid` for the conditions with primary key.

Though currently `path.tableFilter` would be empty now because of the check in https://github.com/pingcap/tidb/blob/45790b5799d535dab0df7b7c6959d947be5f5fe1/planner/core/stats.go#L236, but actually we can relax the condition there to let table path have table filters, so we should consider the `Selection` above this partial table scan here.
We don't need this check anymore, since we have checked `prop.TaskTp` at the beginning of this function.
This function shares a lot of code with `convertToPartialTableScan`, can we extract a common utility function for reuse?
And also with `convertToTableScan`, `convertToPartialIndexScan`, it is better to use small functions that can compose rather than long and repeated codes.
